Imagine asking one friend for advice; they might be wrong. But if you ask many friends, and they all give slightly different opinions, you often get a better answer. This is like combining many simple ideas to make one really strong one. We call this an ensemble.

There are two main ways to build this committee. Imagine many students studying different notes, then voting. This is called Bagging, and it helps fix 'jumpy' mistakes. Or, imagine tutors teaching one after another, each focusing on what the last one got wrong. This is Boosting, which makes 'weak' lessons strong.

With Boosting, we focus on tough problems. Imagine five balloons, all equally weighted. If our first attempt pops just one balloon, that tricky balloon instantly becomes much heavier. So, the next attempt will try extra hard to avoid that specific balloon, learning from the mistake.

Remember, for exams, know how Bagging fixes 'jumpy' problems by reducing variance, and how Boosting strengthens 'weak' lessons by reducing bias. Also, roughly 37 percent of data is 'out-of-bag' in Bagging. Keep practicing these ideas, and you'll do great!
